name.text: Points and a region defined by three inequalities

questiontext.text:
\(R\) is the region where {@ds[1]@}, {@ds[2]@} and {@ds[3]@}. For each point, choose where it is.

  1. \(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]
  2. \(({@P[2][1]@}, {@P[2][2]@})\) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]
  3. \(({@P[3][1]@}, {@P[3][2]@})\) [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]
  4. \(({@P[4][1]@}, {@P[4][2]@})\) [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Substitute each point into all three inequalities. A point is in \(R\) only if it makes every inequality true. A point on a solid edge belongs to \(R\); a point on a dashed edge does not. A point can be on one of the lines and still be outside \(R\).

  1. \(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\): {@vals(1)@}. [[if test="is(cats[1]=1)"]]All three are true and the point is on no line: inside \(R\).[[elif test="is(cats[1]=2)"]]It is on the solid line {@lq(onl[1])@} and satisfies all three: on an edge, included.[[elif test="is(cats[1]=3)"]]It is on the dashed line {@lq(onl[1])@}, which is not included: on an edge, not included.[[else]]It is on the line {@lq(onl[1])@}, but {@ds[brk[1]]@} is false: outside \(R\).[[/if]]

  2. \(({@P[2][1]@}, {@P[2][2]@})\): {@vals(2)@}. [[if test="is(cats[2]=1)"]]All three are true and the point is on no line: inside \(R\).[[elif test="is(cats[2]=2)"]]It is on the solid line {@lq(onl[2])@} and satisfies all three: on an edge, included.[[elif test="is(cats[2]=3)"]]It is on the dashed line {@lq(onl[2])@}, which is not included: on an edge, not included.[[else]]It is on the line {@lq(onl[2])@}, but {@ds[brk[2]]@} is false: outside \(R\).[[/if]]

  3. \(({@P[3][1]@}, {@P[3][2]@})\): {@vals(3)@}. [[if test="is(cats[3]=1)"]]All three are true and the point is on no line: inside \(R\).[[elif test="is(cats[3]=2)"]]It is on the solid line {@lq(onl[3])@} and satisfies all three: on an edge, included.[[elif test="is(cats[3]=3)"]]It is on the dashed line {@lq(onl[3])@}, which is not included: on an edge, not included.[[else]]It is on the line {@lq(onl[3])@}, but {@ds[brk[3]]@} is false: outside \(R\).[[/if]]

  4. \(({@P[4][1]@}, {@P[4][2]@})\): {@vals(4)@}. [[if test="is(cats[4]=1)"]]All three are true and the point is on no line: inside \(R\).[[elif test="is(cats[4]=2)"]]It is on the solid line {@lq(onl[4])@} and satisfies all three: on an edge, included.[[elif test="is(cats[4]=3)"]]It is on the dashed line {@lq(onl[4])@}, which is not included: on an edge, not included.[[else]]It is on the line {@lq(onl[4])@}, but {@ds[brk[4]]@} is false: outside \(R\).[[/if]]

questiondescription.text:
Linear Inequalities: points and a region defined by three inequalities

Grade 12 CBE Essential 1.3: Decide whether points are inside, on an included or excluded edge of, or outside a region defined by three inequalities.

Essential

This question is adapted from Chapter 1 (Graphing inequalities), Section E, question E3(b) of Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP GCSE Mathematics: Higher 2 for AQA, Edexcel and OCR two-tier GCSE mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 2007: new systems and points, with points on solid and dashed edges and on boundary lines outside the region.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: [[if test="is(ans1=\"in\")"]]You chose inside R. Put \(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\) into {@lq(onl[1])@}: the two sides are equal, so the point is on that line. Is the line part of \(R\), and does the point make the other two inequalities true?[[elif test="is(ans1=\"out\") and is(cats[1]=3)"]]\(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\) is not in \(R\), as you say. Now put it into {@lq(onl[1])@}: where exactly is the point?[[elif test="is(ans1=\"out\")"]]You chose outside R. A point outside \(R\) makes at least one inequality false. For \(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\) the three statements are {@vals(1)@}. Is any of them false?[[elif test="is(cats[1]=1)"]]You chose on an edge. A point on an edge makes the two sides of one statement equal. For \(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\) the three statements are {@vals(1)@}. Are two sides equal anywhere?[[elif test="is(cats[1]=4)"]]\(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\) is on the line {@lq(onl[1])@}, as you say. An edge of \(R\) is only the part of that line beside \(R\): does the point make the other two inequalities true?[[else]]\(({@P[1][1]@}, {@P[1][2]@})\) is on the line {@lq(onl[1])@}, as you say. Now read the sign in {@ds[onl[1]]@}: does it allow the two sides to be equal?[[/if]]
